newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Spring says new UK govt must tackle Bloody Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Spring says new UK govt must tackle Bloody Sunday.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said on Wednesday that a new probe into the 1972 Bloody Sunday army slayings of Northern Ireland demonstrators should be "the first thing on the desk" of a new British government.

Spring was speaking on Irish radio days after two British soldiers involved in the shootings cast serious doubt into an official investigation of the incident by the then British chief Justice, Lord Widgery, which exonerated the army.

He said the Dublin government was close to completing a collation of new evidence into the killings at a civil rights march in Londonderry 25 years ago and wanted the British government elected on May 1 to deal with it as a priority.

"There is only a matter of weeks to May 1. I think it is important that we continue our work and make sure that the incoming government will have this to deal with first thing on their desk," Spring said.

Spring said it was clear from statements by two paratroopers who took part in the incident that Widgery's investigation, which found that the soldiers believed they were under fire from IRA guerrillas, was flawed.

One soldier said in a weekend newspaper interview that his platoon was given "shoot to kill" orders the night before the demonstration and that his account of the killings had been torn up and replaced with a fabricated statement.

Another told Britain's Channel 4 news that the soldiers had lost control for a period of 15 minutes. The official version said they believed the Irish Republican Army was shooting at the troops from concealed positions.

The incident was a landmark in Northern Ireland's troubled history and helped turn youths from the 40 percent Catholic minority into supporters of the IRA, which has fought for 28 years to end British rule of the province.

The Irish Foreign Minister said the soldier's account in the Sunday Business Post, in which he said he had seen through his gun sights that the demonstrators were unarmed, was "very damaging and disturbing."

Spring's remarks, and those by Prime Minister John Bruton the previous night from Washington, indicated a determination by the Dublin government to keep Northern Ireland at the top of the agenda of the next British government.

Britain's opposition Labour party seems set to win the election, taking over from a Conservative government whose efforts to end the 28-year conflict have become mired in IRA violence and suspicion from pro-British Unionist groups.

Bruton's administration has led calls for a new investigation and an apology to the families of the 14 dead but Prime Minister John Major's government says that only new evidence will warrant a new probe.

Irish officials believe that the accounts of the two soldiers together with an academic study and tape recordings of intercepted British army radio traffic should be enough to reopen the history books.
